newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC is in a mood to play safe on quotas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC is in a mood to play safe on quotas.

text.p: OPEC was set on Wednesday to take traders' advice and not tamper with its oil quota system, amid uncertainties on how winter weather may affect petroleum demand and about the timing of resumed Iraqi exports.

Ministers of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries met informally in their Vienna hotel suites ahead of a scheduled 1400 GMT start of their 101st ministerial conference about prices and production.
Delegates predicted a Saudi Arabian-led consensus in favour of extending current output quotas, despite rampant violations among the 11 members, at least until June 1997.
Ministers who emerged to say they favoured a "rollover" included Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh, although he also indicated concern about violations.
"I suppose...it is best to keep the current ceiling. It depends on us all being very careful", he said.

Traders say OPEC would be best advised to sidestep issues of market share and alleged cheating, to avoid any public haggling that might alarm a skittish futures market and jeopardise a surprise 1996 rally in world oil prices.
Benchmark Brent Blend crude is trading now around $22.75 a barrel compared with only $18 back in June when OPEC last met.

Prices are firm because of depleted Western stocks of heating fuel ahead of winter, despite the revived prospect that the 1990 Gulf War ban on Iraqi exports may soon be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.

Alleged excess by Venezuela and others is said by Western monitors to have pushed OPEC volume a million barrels a day above a ceiling agreed at 25.03 million barrels per day (BPD), even before the 800,000 bpd extra that has been pencilled in for founder member Iraq begins to flow.

But delegates say that OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia and its Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates feel that the market can absorb even more oil, because stocks are low and as a result of the delay so far on resumed Iraqi sales.

Iraq this week agreed to U.N. conditions that had held up implementing an accord to let it sell $2 billion worth of oil to help buy food and medicine. But details on a pricing formula need to be finalised.

Iraqi chief delegate to the OPEC meeting, which may end on Thursday, told reporters he hoped his oil would flow within weeks. The official, Osama al-Hiti, said that only the pricing formula and "very minor technicalities" had to be ironed out.
Depending on its severity, the northern winter can swing petroleum demand by a million barrels daily, Barclays Bank economists note in heir latest Commodities Survey.

The Barclays analysts have revised up their forecast for average 1996 oil prices to $20 per barrel from only $16.8 in 1995. But they add that "our view remains that prices are likely to ease next year".

The expectation that they'll be weaker by perhaps one dollar is based on the "strong possibility" of revived Iraqi exports and a prospect of increased supply from the North Sea, Asia and Latin America.
